value.question: Combine evidence from at least two sources on why single-request transformer inference is memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound.

steps.description: Search the web for primary sources (academic papers like Korthikanti et al. 2023 or Pope et al. 2022, NVIDIA technical blogs, framework docs) explaining why single-request transformer inference is memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound, focusing on the arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) of autoregressive token-by-token decoding.

Fetch and verify at least two primary pages to confirm quantitative evidence such as the FLOPs-per-token versus the weight-bytes-loaded-per-token ratio for representative model sizes (e.g., a 7B-parameter model reading ~14 GB of weights per generated token).

Calculate a representative arithmetic-intensity example for a single-token decode step (e.g., 7B-parameter model: FLOPs per token vs bytes of weights loaded per token), then compare that intensity against a machine's compute-to-memory-bandwidth ratio to demonstrate that bandwidth, not FLOPs, is the limiting factor; state the expected output numbers.

key_findings: Single-request (no-batch / decode) transformer inference is memory-bandwidth bound because, for each generated token, the entire set of model weights must be loaded from VRAM and used in a full forward pass, so the memory traffic from loading the weights and the KV cache exceeds the computation time (web-b3ba7ab94716; web-05b4d2e5da74).

The memory-bound nature is explained by arithmetic intensity: decode has low arithmetic intensity—relatively few floating-point operations are needed compared to loading the entire model weights—whereas high-intensity workloads (like prefill, which performs massive attention computations across thousands of tokens) are compute-bound on the same hardware (fetch-02568fc45834; web-65b28fce72c3; fetch-eaa6e11fe799).

Because the bottleneck is memory bandwidth rather than compute, no amount of compute optimization will make single-request decode faster; instead, the standard mitigation is batching multiple requests together, which increases the compute performed for the same amount of memory traffic and shifts the workload away from being memory bound (fetch-eaa6e11fe799; fetch-02568fc45834).
gaps: The evidence does not provide a fully worked numeric example of the decode-step arithmetic intensity calculation (e.g., the d=128, N=4096 example is cut off), so the exact ops:byte comparison for a specific model and GPU is not established in the fetched material.

The evidence does not quantify how much memory traffic is attributable to model weights versus KV cache separately for the single-request decode case, nor does it specify the threshold arithmetic intensity at which a given transformer decode workload transitions from memory-bound to compute-bound.

value.answer: Single-request transformer inference is memory-bandwidth bound because, for each generated token, the entire model weights must be loaded from VRAM and used in a full forward pass, so memory traffic from weights and the KV cache exceeds computation time; no-batch inference is well established as memory-bound. This reflects low arithmetic intensity in decode: relatively few floating-point operations are needed compared to loading the entire model weights, whereas high-intensity prefill is compute-bound on the same hardware. Because the bottleneck is bandwidth rather than compute, no compute optimization will make single-request decode faster; the standard mitigation is batching, which performs more compute for the same memory traffic.
key_points: For each generated token in single-request decode, the entire model weights must be loaded from VRAM and used in a full forward pass, so weight plus KV-cache memory traffic exceeds computation time.
Decode has low arithmetic intensity—few FLOPs relative to bytes of weights loaded—making it memory-bound, while high-intensity prefill is compute-bound on the same hardware.

Because bandwidth is the bottleneck, compute optimization cannot speed up single-request decode; batching more requests increases compute for the same memory traffic and shifts the workload away from being memory bound.
